note: The 24 checkpoint-after-fill documents judged again on 2026-09-08 in one sitting, immediately after the before set; compare `now` against 2026-09-08-rejudge-checkpoint-before-2.json.

then.rationale: Integrity and legibility hold: no clipping, no placeholder text, headers/footers ('Confidential — Client Only', page x/5, 8 September 2026) repeat consistently, and the blue rule under each section title plus the eyebrow ('Repositioning Assessment | Heritage Foods') repeat identically across pages 2–5, so the system reads as a system. Where it fails is level 4 — communicative effectiveness. The document is five pages of almost nothing but body prose: pages 2, 3 and 5 are single columns of paragraphs occupying roughly the top third of the sheet with two-thirds of each page left blank, and page 5 in particular carries one short 'What Would Change This' paragraph plus a one-line 'Notes and sources' footnote across an otherwise empty A4 page — that page should have been folded into page 4 or filled. Page 3, 'The Two Paths', is the analytical heart of the brief (narrow the gap vs premiumise) and is rendered as two undifferentiated prose paragraphs with a small indented 'About the price gap' aside; there is no comparison table, no side-by-side of the two options, nothing that lets the marketing director see the trade-off at a glance. There are no charts anywhere despite share loss over three years, a widening 38% gap and a 61% under-40 growth stat all being plot-ready. The only visual device in the whole deck is the three-stat band on page 4 (−4pts / 38% / 61%), which is well built — units set, sub-labels present, one source line beneath — but it is the sole piece of information design in five pages, and it repeats numbers already stated in the page-2 body. Section titles are also labels rather than conclusions: 'Situation', 'The Two Paths', 'Evidence' say nothing; only 'Recommendation' carries an argument, and even there the finding lives in the paragraph, not the heading. Genericness is moderate rather than severe: the content is clearly written for this brief (private label, under-40 cohort, price-gap arithmetic), but the container — cover with rule, eyebrow, section title, body block — would look identical for any consulting memo on any subject; the stat band on page 4 is the only element that could not be lifted wholesale into another document. Not sendable unchanged: the empty lower two-thirds of pages 2, 3 and 5 and the absence of any comparison of the two options would read as an unfinished draft.

Integrity and legibility hold: no clipping, no placeholder text, consistent running head ("Repositioning Assessment: Defending Share Without Losing the Brand") and footer ("Confidential — internal use", folio, date) on pages 2–5, and a consistent title/rule/body rhythm. Where it stops short is density and structure against the purpose. Four of the five pages die well before the bottom margin: page 2 ends mid-page after three takeaway bullets, the pull paragraph and two short paragraphs, leaving roughly the bottom half blank; page 3's text stops around two-thirds down; page 5's recommendation plus the "Notes and sources" list with a single entry leaves more than half the page empty. The cover (page 1) puts eyebrow, title, subtitle, date and confidentiality line in the top quarter and abandons the rest. For an assessment built on 4 points of share loss, a 38% price gap and 61% of category growth, there is not one chart or table anywhere — the only quantitative treatment is the three-stat row on page 4 (-4 pts / 38% / 61%), which is well captioned and sourced but is doing the work a share-trend or option-comparison exhibit should be doing, and the two options on page 4 are argued in running prose rather than laid side by side. Titles do earn their keep ("The brand's problem is relevance, not price"; "Two strategies, one converging deadline"), and the recommendation page names the falsifying evidence, so the argument is sound; the artefact around it is under-built. Visually it is a neutral consulting shell — hairline rules, one accent line on the cover, single-column text — that would look identical for a logistics or insurance brief with the words swapped.

Integrity holds: no clipped text, no placeholder strings, no overlaps; the cover (p1), the three stat blocks on p4 (4pts / 38% / 61%), and the footer rule with page numbers and date all render cleanly. Legibility is fine at document scale, and the running header (title left, section word right) plus the blue rule under each heading repeat consistently across pp2-7, so visual coherence is met. It fails at level 4 on page-fill and communicative structure: pages 2, 3, 5, 6 and 7 all stop between one third and one half down the page, leaving 50-65% of each sheet blank with no visual element to carry it — p5 'Recommendation' is a single 12-line paragraph occupying the top fifth of a page, and p7 'Immediate next steps' is three bullets plus a one-line source note on an otherwise empty page. For an assessment built on share, price gap and growth-by-cohort data, there is not a single chart or table anywhere in seven pages; the 4pt share loss over three years, the 38% gap widening, and the under-40 growth split are all asserted in prose on p2 and p3 where a trend line and a cohort bar would do the work. Page 4 'Two paths forward' is the strongest page — the three-stat row with unit-carrying labels and a source line beneath — but it presents only the numbers, not the two options side by side, so the recommended path is never visually contrasted with the rejected one. Titles are decent conclusions ('Why the share is being lost', 'What would change this recommendation'), which is why it clears the bar for coherence but not effectiveness. Genericness: apart from the small brand mark on the cover and the one accent colour, this is the default Word-report chassis — title / rule / body column, no distinctive typographic system or layout idea; swap the words and it serves any category review.

Integrity holds: no clipped or placeholder text on any of the five pages, and the header/footer furniture (running title, section label right-aligned, 'Confidential — Internal', page x/5, date) repeats identically on pages 2-5. Legibility is fine at print size, though the body measure on pages 2-5 is narrow relative to the huge right margin — every page leaves roughly 45-50% of the page empty below the content, which is the main craft failure. Coherence is consistent: same blue rule under each H1, same section-label convention, same left-aligned single column. Communicative effectiveness is genuinely good and is where the document earns its level: page 2's title 'The programme is €9m behind plan at month 14' is a conclusion, not a label; page 3 'Property and IT are stalled on unowned decisions' names the cause; page 4 'Half the shortfall closes with three decisions' carries the recommendation and backs it with a three-figure stat strip (19€m banked / 9€m shortfall / 4.5€m recoverable) with units and labels under each; the named decisions carry owners (Head of Corporate Real Estate, CIO, Programme Sponsor/COO); page 5 states the do-nothing landing point (€33m against €46m, 28% miss) as its title. The 'Definition' callout for 'blocked on ownership' on page 3 is a thoughtful, brief-specific touch. What stops this shipping: there is not a single chart or table in a review whose whole argument is workstream-level delivery against target (118% / 41% / 33% against a €28m plan) — that comparison is asserted in prose on pages 2-3 and never shown, so the reader must reconstruct it; page 3 in particular is four paragraphs of unbroken text where a three-row workstream table belongs. The page-fill imbalance compounds this: pages 2, 3 and 5 each end at roughly half height, so there was room for the evidence. Page 5 is especially thin — a short paragraph plus a one-item 'Notes and sources' list ('Programme finance tracker, month 14') on an otherwise blank page. Not generic in language — the copy is written for this brief and the stat strip is specific — but the visual system (blue rule, single column, stat row) would sit unchanged under any other consulting title.

Integrity holds: no clipped or placeholder text on any of the five pages; the page 3 bar chart, the page 4 workstream table and the page 5 numbered decision list all render fully. Legibility is adequate but marginal in places — page 4's table type and the footnote-styled 'Methodological note' box sit noticeably smaller than surrounding body copy, and the page 2 KPI sub-labels ('Procurement vs target', 'Property vs target', 'IT vs target') are small enough to strain at print size. Coherence is the strongest layer: the blue rule under the eyebrow, the running header (topic left / section right), the footer triad (confidential / page / date) and the single accent blue repeat identically across pages 2-5, and the H1 sits on a consistent baseline throughout. Where it stops short of level 4 is communicative fit. Page 2's three KPI figures are the programme's headline evidence but they are stated as bare percentages of target with delta 'pts' and no euro anchor, so the €19m vs €28m spine of the brief never appears as a number in the KPI band — the reader has to mine it out of the paragraph below. The page 3 chart is the weakest element: a three-bar chart of 118/41/33 carries no information the sentence above it doesn't already carry, its y-axis runs to 125% with no target reference line at 100, and its caption ('Two blocked decisions, not a shortage of savings ideas') is a claim the chart cannot support. Page 4's table has an unlabelled 'Recoverable' column — 2.5 and 2.0 with no unit in the header, only recoverable from the surrounding prose as €m — which is exactly the kind of unstated unit that breaks a finance table. Page 5 carries the strongest content, naming the three decisions with owners and 30 September dates, but it is set as plain numbered text with no owner/date column structure, so the accountability the brief asked to foreground reads as paragraph rather than commitment. Pages 3 and 4 are also visibly under-filled — roughly half the page height is white below the last element — while page 5's substance is squeezed into the top third, which reads as flow rather than composition. Distinctiveness: the type and rule system are competent and restrained, but nothing in the layout is specific to a cost programme; swap the words and this is a generic corporate review shell.

Integrity holds: no clipping, no placeholder text, the page-3 bar chart, the page-4 recovery table and the page-2 stat row all render fully. Legibility is fine at document size — the header/footer rules, the small caps section labels (Overview, Workstreams, Recovery, Outlook, Actions) and the body text all read cleanly, and reading order is unambiguous. Visual coherence is genuinely good: the same blue rule under the page header, the same footer triplet (Confidential — Steering Committee / page / September 2026), the same title-then-rule pattern and the same caption/source treatment repeat on every content page.

It fails at level 4 on density and page discipline. Page 3 stops around a third of the way down and leaves the bottom two-thirds blank; page 4 stops after the three-row recovery table and one 'Basis of estimate' note, leaving roughly three-quarters of the sheet empty; page 5 ('If nothing changes') carries one four-line paragraph and a three-item 'Notes and sources' list and is then blank for the rest of the page; page 6 ('What the transformation office should do') ends after the three bullets and one closing paragraph with more than half the page unused. Four of six pages are under-filled, which makes a six-page review out of what is really two or three pages of argument and breaks the rhythm the rest of the document establishes. Page 5 is the worst offender — the most consequential section of the brief (what the programme lands at if nothing changes: EUR 33m against EUR 46m) is a single paragraph floating on an otherwise empty sheet, given less visual weight than the routine recovery table on page 4.

Content-wise it does the brief's work: page 2 states the 19.0m/118%/41%/33% figures with units, page 3's chart has a figure number, a takeaway line ('The shortfall is concentrated in two workstreams') and a PMO source, page 4 names three decisions with owners and EUR amounts, page 6 names dates and owners. Titles are conclusions rather than labels ('A programme carrying two workstreams, not five', 'Half the shortfall is recoverable this quarter'). That content specificity is why it is not maximally generic, but the shell — blue accent, thin rules, single-column body, one bar chart, one three-row table — would look identical for any other cost review; nothing about the composition is designed around this programme's two-blocked-workstreams story.

I would not send this unchanged: a client reading page 5 would see the punchline of the review stranded in white space.

Integrity and legibility hold: no clipping, no placeholder text, headers ('CSRD Readiness Assessment' left, section name right) and the footer triad (Confidential — Audit Committee / page x of 7 / 8 September 2026) repeat correctly on pages 2–7, and the blue rule under each H1 plus the blue accent bar on the page-1 title block are used consistently. Where it fails is level 4, on density and page discipline. Page 5 ('What to build first') carries one four-item numbered list ending around a third down, leaving roughly two-thirds of the sheet blank. Page 4 ('Scope 3: the critical gap') ends after the three-row materiality/availability table and the boxed method note at about half height. Page 6 stops after the 'What the first report will not be able to say' bullets with the lower half empty, and page 7 is the worst offender — a two-sentence recommendation and a two-item 'Notes and sources' list occupy the top quarter and then nothing. Four of seven pages read as half-finished, and the reader gets no signal whether that is a section break or the end. The page-3 chart is also thin for the space it claims: three bars (34/29/19) restate the exact three stat blocks already given on page 2, so a full-width figure with axis, legend, caption and source is spent on a number the reader has already been handed — and the y-axis 'Datapoints (of 82)' plus the caption/source line are the only things earning their keep. On the credit side, titles do conclude ('Scope 3: the critical gap', 'What to estimate, and what we honestly can't say yet'), the chart and table both carry a source line ('Internal CSRD datapoint gap assessment, Sept 2026'), and the page-2 stat row with its 'Already collected / Collectable this year / Need new measurement' labels is the strongest element in the document. Genericness: the prose is unmistakably written for this brief — 82 datapoints, the 34/29/19 split, spend-based Scope 3 estimation, named data owners, phased build — but the visual system is a stock corporate-report shell (single blue accent, serif-free body, rule-under-heading, three-part footer) that would look identical for a tax memo or a pension review; nothing in the composition is derived from the readiness/gap subject except the one bar chart.

Integrity holds: no clipping, no placeholder text, the chart on page 3 and the table on page 4 both render fully, headers/footers ('CSRD Readiness Assessment' / section word / 'Confidential — Audit Committee' / x of 5 / date) repeat cleanly on pages 2-5. Legibility is fine for a print/PDF audit-committee read, and the reading order is unambiguous single-column. Coherence is good: the blue rule under every heading, the same section-word marker, consistent caption/source micro-type. Communication is genuinely strong — every page title is a conclusion ('Two-thirds of required datapoints are already within reach', 'Nineteen datapoints should be disclosed as estimates, not measured'), the 41%/35%/23% trio on page 2 carries labels and a dated source line, the page 3 bar chart has a figure caption, an explicit takeaway ('Target the 29 collectable datapoints first...') and a source, the page 4 table gives datapoint counts and a method column, and page 5 closes with numbered notes and sources. What stops it at 4 rather than 5, and what stops me sending it: the vertical rhythm is broken by repeated half-empty pages. Page 2 ends roughly at mid-page with a large blank lower half after the body paragraph, page 4 likewise stops after the 'Estimation, not evasion' callout leaving the bottom 45% empty, and page 5 — the honest-limits conclusion, arguably the most important page — is barely a third full above the notes. Page 3 alone is properly filled. The cover is also thin: a rule, title, one-line subtitle, date and confidentiality stamp on an otherwise empty A4, with no anchoring of the 82/34/29/19 framing that the rest of the document runs on. The page 3 chart also carries a legend ('ESRS datapoints by readiness') for a single series, which is redundant next to the axis label. Not generic content — the stat trio, the readiness bar chart and the estimation-basis table are all built from this brief's numbers — but the shell around them (cover, heading rule, body-then-figure-then-body cadence) is a general-purpose report frame that would look identical for a different topic.

Integrity and legibility hold: no clipping, no placeholder text, consistent 9pt-ish body, the blue rule under the running head and the 'CSRD Readiness Assessment / [section] ' header plus 'Confidential — Audit Committee / n / 9 / 3 September 2026' footer repeat identically on pages 2-9, and the title block on page 1 is cleanly set. Coherence is real: heading size, the hairline under each H1, the indented pull-block on pages 2 and 3, and the left-aligned single measure agree throughout. It stops at 3 on density and fit for purpose. Pages 6, 7, 8 and 9 each carry only three or four short paragraphs and then leave roughly two-thirds of the page blank — 'What to Build First' (p6) ends at about 40% depth, 'What the First Report Will Not Be Able to Say' (p8) and 'Recommended Roadmap and Governance' (p9) the same — so the rhythm collapses in the back half and the reader gets an obviously underfilled sheet four times running. The brief is intrinsically tabular (82 datapoints split 34/29/19, per-datapoint owner and first measurement date, a build sequence, a Scope 3 category screen) and none of that is ever tabulated: the 34/29/19 stat trio on page 4 is the only non-prose device in nine pages, and even it is followed by more paragraph. There is no chart, no roadmap table with dates, no list of the 19 uninstrumented datapoints — the 'notes and sources' on page 9 is a single one-item numbered list. Page 5, 'Scope 3 Emissions: The Critical Gap', is the highest-stakes section and is delivered as one unbroken 12-line paragraph with the fifteen-category screen described in running text rather than shown. Genericness: the wording is tightly specific to this manufacturer, but the visual system — one accent rule, one column, one stat row, no marks or data display — would render an identical-looking document for any other assessment brief.

Integrity holds: no clipped text, no placeholders, headers/footers ('Nordic Sales Office: Market Entry Assessment' left, section tag right, 'Confidential — Board Use Only / x / 5 / 8 September 2026' foot) render on every page. Legibility is fine for print — body copy, the key-takeaways bullets on p2 and the p4 table are all readable, and the single blue accent rule under each H1 gives an obvious reading order. Coherence is consistent: same title rule, same section eyebrow, same footer triplet on p2–5, and the p4 stat row (2.1 €m / 26mo / 34mo) uses the same type family as everything else. Where it drops is communicative fit: every one of pages 2, 3, 4 and 5 stops around the 45–50% mark and leaves the bottom half of the page blank — p3 ends after two short paragraphs and the 'Market definition' callout, p5 ends after three numbered conditions plus a three-item notes list, so the document is a five-page shell carrying roughly two-and-a-half pages of content. The brief asked to show payback under both cases and the deliverable does it entirely in prose plus a three-row table on p4; with that much empty page below, a payback/break-even chart on p4 was both possible and expected. Titles do earn their keep ('Enter now: the Nordic gap in Finnish-language scheduling software is winnable', 'The Stockholm office pays back within three years under both cases'), units are attached (EUR 2.1m, Month 26, 25 months), and each exhibit carries a source line, which is why this sits at 3 rather than lower. Craft is not there: the p4 stat trio and the p2 bullets are the only compositional moves, and the p5 notes list sits orphaned above half a blank page.

Integrity and legibility hold: no clipping, no placeholder text, consistent running head ("Nordic Market Entry Assessment" left, section label right) and footer ("Confidential — Board", page x of 5, date) on pages 2–5, and the cover on page 1 is clean with its navy rule above "Board of Directors". Typography is coherent — same navy H1 with underrule, same body size, the "Key takeaways" bullet block on page 2 and the "Sizing basis" callout on page 3 both read as deliberate variants of one system. Where it fails is density and evidence. Page 4 is titled "The investment pays back within three years under either scenario" but the only artefact is three inline stat figures (2.1 €m / 26mo / 34mo) and two short paragraphs; the brief explicitly asked to show payback under both cases and there is no chart, no timeline, no cumulative-cashflow table anywhere in the document. Likewise page 3 asserts EUR 340m across four countries growing 9% and 61% incumbent share entirely in prose — no country split table, no share breakdown. The consequence is visible on the contact sheet: page 3 ends about 45% down the page, page 4 about 40%, page 5 about 35%, leaving more than half of three of the five pages blank. A five-page board pack that leaves that much air while omitting the two exhibits the board would ask for is not one I would hand over unchanged. Titles are genuinely conclusion-shaped and the page-5 numbered conditions are specific (Finnish-language delivery before Finland sales, Stockholm country lead by month 3, reference hospital group in four quarters), which lifts it above pure boilerplate, but the visual treatment — single column, navy accent, generic stat row — would look identical for any other market-entry brief.

Integrity and legibility hold: no clipping, overlap or placeholder text anywhere, the header/footer rules and eyebrow labels (Market, Competition, Economics, Payback, Conditions, Recommendation) repeat exactly, and the section title + underline treatment is identical on pages 2-7, so visual coherence is met. It fails at communicative effectiveness on density. Page 6, 'Conditions the recommendation depends on', is three short bullets occupying the top ~20% of the sheet with roughly four-fifths of the page blank — and these are the three conditions the brief asked to be named, so the most load-bearing page is the emptiest. Page 4 stops after the four-row investment table and the small 'Methodology' callout, leaving the bottom ~45% empty; page 2 ends after the 340€m / 9% / 61% stat trio and one paragraph with a similar void; page 7, the recommendation, ends at about half height. Page 5's payback line chart is drawn small in the upper third with tiny axis labels ('Month 0 (launch)', 'Month 18', 'Month 26', 'Month 34') and the negative cumulative-cash values are hard to read at that scale, while the space below it sits unused — the one exhibit the board will look at hardest is under-sized on a half-empty page. Charts do carry figure captions with a takeaway and a source line (Figure 1 on page 3, Figure 2 on page 5) and units are present (EUR m, months, %), which is why this clears the lower bars. Genericness: the stat trio, the methodology callout and the conditions section are shaped to this brief, but the title page, rules and section furniture would read the same for any market-entry deck.

Integrity and legibility hold: no clipping, no placeholder text, headers ('Integration Assessment: Post-Acquisition Sequencing') and footers ('Confidential — Steering Committee Only | 8 September 2026') repeat identically on pages 2-5, and the body/heading scale is consistent. Communicatively it is strong for a steering-committee read: page 2's title 'Overlap and scale make an EUR 8.2m synergy case' states a conclusion and the 31% / 12/41 / EUR 8.2m stat trio is labelled with units; page 3's bar chart carries a numbered figure caption, an explicit takeaway sentence ('The remaining EUR 3.3m stays at zero on this curve until both companies dispatch from one system') and a source line; page 4's phase table has a units-bearing header ('Depots merged', 'Dispatch sites') plus a source, and page 5 answers the deferral question directly ('Deferring the migration a year forfeits EUR 3.3m, not delays it'). What stops it at 4 and stops me sending it is page fill. Page 5 ends its bullet list and 'Notes and sources' block at roughly the vertical midpoint, leaving the entire bottom half of the page blank — it reads as a document that ran out rather than closed. Pages 2, 3 and 4 each also leave a blank bottom third (page 2's last paragraph ends well above the footer; page 3's chart is small in its frame with a large gap between the closing paragraph and the footer), so the rhythm across the deck is top-weighted rather than composed. The chart itself is minimal craft: three bars, one series, and a legend entry ('Synergy achievable without migration') that duplicates what the axis title already says. Genericness is middling: the numbers, milestone phases and the depot/dispatch language are unmistakably this brief, but the shell — thin blue rule under the cover title, single accent blue, generic stat trio, plain grey table header — would carry any other assessment unchanged.

Integrity holds across all six pages: no clipped text, no placeholder strings, no overlap; the page 3 chart, the page 4 checkpoint table and the page 6 callout box all sit inside their measures, and every page carries the same running header/footer pair. Legibility is fine for a printed committee read — body copy is generous, the blue rule under 'Executive summary'/'Overlap and synergy profile' etc. gives a consistent entry point, and reading order is single-column and obvious. Coherence is strong: identical header band, the same left-aligned H1 with underline, the same small-caps 'Notes and sources' treatment on page 6, and the KPI strip on page 2 (8.2€m / 31% / 12/41) is the only band element and is not repeated arbitrarily. Communicative effectiveness is where it earns the level — titles conclude rather than label ('What deferring the system migration a year costs', 'Month 6 — Fund the critical path, protect the overlap'), the page 3 figure has a numbered caption with a takeaway and a source line, the page 4 table has a source note plus a 'Critical path' callout, and the units are on the numbers (EUR 8.2m, EUR 3.3m, 12 of 41 depots). What keeps it off 5: the page 3 chart is a two-bar comparison that carries almost no information the sentence above it doesn't already carry, and its y-axis label 'Annual synergy (€m)' with only two categories wastes half a page; page 1 is an otherwise empty cover with a small title block floating at mid-height, and pages 4 and 5 leave large bottom whitespace, so the six-page pacing is uneven rather than composed. It is not generic — the milestone headings, the deferral arithmetic on page 6 and the checkpoint table are written for this deal, not for any deal — but the underlying frame (rule-under-title, KPI strip, notes-and-sources) is a recognisable consulting shell.

Integrity, legibility and coherence hold: the blue rule + running head/footer repeat identically on pages 2-5, the KPI trio on page 2 (31% / 12/41 / EUR 8.2m) sits on a clean three-column rhythm, and the page-3 chart carries an axis label (annual run-rate EUR m), a legend, a Figure 1 takeaway caption and a dated source line. Communicatively it is strong for the brief: every title is a conclusion rather than a label ('Synergy is real but 40% rides on one unbudgeted system', 'A year's delay defers EUR 3.3m of synergy'), the page-4 table decomposes 3.3 + 1.6 + 3.3 against M1-6 / M7-18 / M19-24 with a method note explaining run-rate vs cash, and the six-month milestones are named as a four-step sequence. It stops short of level 5 on two visible defects: the 'Notes and sources' list on page 5 is numbered 1. then 3. — the second marker is skipped, which is exactly the kind of error a steering committee spots; and page 5 ends at roughly the halfway mark, leaving the closing recommendation floating over a half-empty page, while the page-1 cover also leaves the lower two-thirds blank. Fix the footnote numbering and the last-page fall and it ships; not unchanged.

Integrity holds: no clipping, no placeholder text, no overlaps; the KPI strip on p2, the bar chart on p3 and the tier table on p4 all render. Legibility is adequate at print size, and the running header/footer repeat consistently across pp2-5. Coherence is decent — the blue rule under the H1, the caption style under the chart, and the header/footer band repeat without hand-placement. Where it falls down is level 4 and page economy. The whole review is five pages but pp3, 4 and 5 each use only the top third of the sheet and leave more than half the page empty; p5 in particular has one paragraph, a three-item sources list, and roughly 60% white space below it, which reads as an unfinished page rather than a deliberate closing. The chart on p3 is the weakest element: three segments with only two visible bars (the 'below cost' and 'near cost' bars are near-zero and the 'top 15%' bar dominates), a y-axis running to 40 with no percent framing beyond the axis label, and a single-series legend that adds nothing — for a three-tier margin story the reader has to reconstruct the tiers from the caption text rather than the chart. The brief's core numbers are present (19%, 22%, 12%/40%/34%, churn per tier, nine-month runway, the two-largest-accounts contingency on p5) and titles are conclusion-shaped ('Three years without repricing cut gross margin from 31% to 19%', 'A three-tier reprice recovers margin over nine months'), which is genuinely good. But the tier table on p4 has no source line adjacent to it in the same way the chart does, and the churn ranges ('9-14%', '5-8%', '3-5%') are given without saying whether that is accounts or revenue. Not distinctive: the single-accent-blue-rule-on-white treatment with a bare cover page (title, subtitle, three metadata lines, nothing else) would fit any consulting memo; the only brief-specific design decision is the KPI triptych on p2. Would not send unchanged — the page-fill problem on pp3-5 and the near-useless chart are the blockers.

Integrity holds: no clipped text, no placeholders, no overlap; page 1 cover, the p3 bar chart and the p4/p5/p6 tables all render fully. Legibility is adequate for print, though the p3 chart axis labels and the small-caps eyebrows ('Executive Summary', 'Diagnosis', 'Repricing') sit near the bottom of comfortable size, and the p5/p6 table body type is noticeably smaller than the surrounding paragraphs. Coherence is largely met — consistent running header/footer, one accent blue, one rule under each H1, consistent table styling. Where it falls short of level 4 is communicative effectiveness. Page 2's three KPI figures ('19.0', '31.0', '22.0') carry no unit on the number itself — 19.0 and 31.0 are percentages and 22.0 is a percentage rise in cost, all rendered identically, so the reader must decode them from the caption line beneath. The p3 chart is a three-bar series of a single metric, which is a table pretending to be a chart, and its title 'The Margin Problem' states a topic rather than the conclusion the caption actually carries ('margin fell 31% to 19% while cost rose'). Pages 5, 6 and 7 are roughly one-third full — the three-tier plan, the churn table and the two-largest-accounts contingency each end mid-page with a large empty lower half, which for the central recommendation of the review reads as under-built rather than airy. Page 4's 'Account Segmentation by Margin' table has only three rows and does not reconcile to 100% of the book, leaving the 33% unaccounted for that the p4 body text mentions but the table does not show. Page 8's recommendation is four bullets plus a numbered source list, which is thin for the closing page. Genericness: the only brief-specific visual is the single bar chart; everything else is heading, paragraph, table, callout box in a default serif/sans pairing that would read identically for a marketing plan or an IT review. Nothing in the composition is shaped by pricing tiers, churn bands or the account-concentration story — no tier ladder, no waterfall from 31% to 19%, no concentration visual for the two largest accounts. I would not send this unchanged: the half-empty recommendation pages and the unitless KPIs would draw comment from a commercial director.

Integrity and legibility hold: no clipping, overlap or placeholder text anywhere; the running header ("Pricing Review: Restoring Margin Without Losing the Book" left, section word right) and the three-part footer repeat identically on pages 2-7, and the blue rule under each H1 plus the blue section eyebrow are consistent. Type is a single serif/sans pairing at stable sizes; the KPI trio on page 2 (19% / 22% / 12%) is the only display-scale type and it is used once, deliberately. So levels 1-3 are met.

Level 4 fails on density. Pages 5, 6 and 7 are each roughly three-quarters empty. Page 5 "Expected Churn by Tier" is a single five-line paragraph carrying the 15-20% / 3-8% / 2-4% churn numbers with no table, even though the same content on page 4 was given a three-row tier table — the repricing schedule table exists but its churn counterpart does not, so the reader cannot line the two up. Page 6 "The Two Largest Accounts" is one paragraph plus a small "If either refuses" callout box and then half a page of nothing. Page 7 "Recommendation" is one paragraph and a three-item "Notes and sources" list, ending the document on a visually empty page. In a seven-page review, three pages that stop a third of the way down read as unfinished rather than airy.

The chart on page 3 is also weak as evidence: only the "Top 15% by revenue" bar reads at all; the "Below cost (12%)" and "Within 2 pts (40%)" categories are flat against the axis, so the chart shows one number rather than the spread the caption claims ("more than half the book sits at or within two points of cost"). The caption itself is done correctly — figure number, takeaway sentence and a source line — as is the table source note on page 4.

Not shippable unchanged: I would not put my name on a document whose last three pages are mostly white space, and I would rebuild the churn page as a table.

On genericness: the writing is clearly for this brief (fuel/driver cost inflation, the named tier timings Mo. 1-3 / 3-7 / 7-9, the "named negotiation track" fallback), and the "If either refuses" callout is a real editorial choice. But the visual system — white page, one blue accent, rule-under-heading, centred footer triplet — is the default consulting-report look and would survive unchanged on any other subject.

Integrity and legibility hold: no clipping, overlap or placeholder text on any of the six pages, and the header/footer band (document title left, section label right, 'Internal — Executive briefing / page / September 2026') repeats correctly. Coherence is also largely intact — the blue rule under each page title, the three-up KPI band on p2 (210,000 / €6.40 / €1.34M) and p5 (€477K / €280K / <7 mo), and the caption+source pattern under the p3 chart and p4 table all repeat in the same style. Titles are conclusive rather than topical ('Counters cost nearly five times the average contact', 'A redesigned model can save about €477,000 a year'), the p3 figure carries a numbered caption, a takeaway line and a source, and the p4 table carries both a source and a method note qualifying the €4.80 self-service-eligible average — that is real rigour. What blocks level 4 is density and pagination. Page 2 stops roughly 55% down the page: after the €1.34M KPI band and two short paragraphs the lower ~45% is blank, so the opening findings page reads as a half-used sheet. Page 6 is worse — it is a spill page holding four bullets, the 'Commitment' box and the notes/sources list, occupying under a third of the sheet; the 'Who loses access' argument on p5 is left running over a page break into an almost empty page. Page 5 is the opposite problem: the italic mitigation paragraph plus two bullet stacks and the KPI band push it to the bottom margin, so p5 and p6 together look unbalanced rather than composed. The p3 chart is also weak for the page it owns: three bars, one of which ('Blended average') duplicates what the legend line 'Average cost per contact' already asserts, in a plot occupying maybe a third of the text column while the page has room for a far more legible comparison. Craft-wise this is a competent but conventional brief-report shell — cover, KPI trio, one chart, one table — with the brief's numbers dropped in; nothing in the composition is specific to a transport authority.

Integrity holds: no clipping, overlap or placeholder text on any of the five pages; the page 3 bar chart, the page 4 savings table and the page 5 exclusion list all render fully inside the text column. Legibility is fine for A4 reading — the page 2 KPI row (1.34 €m / 24.80 € / 44%) is the only display type and it reads cleanly, and reading order is single-column and obvious. Coherence is good: the same blue hairline under the section title, the same running header ("Redesigning Contact Channels: A Self-Service-First Model" left, section tag right) and the same three-part footer ("Confidential — Executive Review" / page x of 5 / date) repeat on pages 2-5, and the eyebrow-plus-rule device on page 1 matches the section rule inside. Communication is genuinely strong: every section title states a conclusion ("Counters cost nearly four times the network average", "A self-service-first model saves an estimated €500,000 a year"), the page 3 chart carries a numbered caption, a takeaway line and a source, the page 4 table has a units row (Saving €/yr, % of cost) plus a boxed methods note, and the brief's brutal part — passengers who lose counter access — gets its own page 5 with a seven-item list and the transition cost (€280,000) and payback. Level 5 fails on page fill and finish: page 3 ends just past the halfway mark leaving a third of the sheet blank under the chart caption, page 4 stops right after the methods box with nearly half the page empty, and page 5 leaves a similar band under "Notes and sources" — three of four content pages are short because each section is forced onto a fresh page, which reads as an unresolved template flow rather than a composed document. The page 2 body is also one undifferentiated 12-line paragraph immediately under the KPI band, which is the densest and least designed block in the set. Clean and defensible, but I would rebalance the section breaks before putting my name on it.

Integrity holds: no clipping, no placeholder text, and the running head (document title left, section label right), the '01'–'06' section markers and the footer triad ('internal use only' / x of 7 / 8 September 2026) repeat identically on pages 2–7, so hierarchy and rhythm are consistent. Legibility is adequate for an A4 executive read, and the reading order is unambiguous. It fails at level 4 on density and evidence design. Every content page stops well short of the bottom: page 3 ('Where the Cost and the Opportunity Sit') ends after the 'Method note' box at roughly 45% of the page, page 4 ends after the paragraph under the 92,400 / 60% / 4.80€ stat row at about half height, page 7 ('Recommendation and Next Steps') ends after the two-item 'Notes and sources' list at about a third of the page, and pages 2, 5 and 6 all leave 35–55% empty below the last line. Seven pages carry maybe four pages of content, and the whitespace is uniform trailing dead space rather than a deliberate device. The analytic core of the brief — 44% of contacts in three question types, counters at 8% of contacts but 31% of cost — is never drawn: there is no chart anywhere in the document, only the stat trio on page 4 and the 'Illustrative savings calculation' table on page 5. That cost-versus-volume asymmetry is the one number an executive board needs to see at a glance, and it is left in prose on page 3. Credit where due: the page 5 table carries units on every row (EUR 6.40, EUR 226,000 / yr, '< 1 year') and a source line, the stat row on page 4 has a source note, and page 6 ('Who Loses Access If Counters Close') answers the brief's equity requirement explicitly with a nine-item exclusion list and an 'Equity safeguard' note. Titles are descriptive but only half conclude — 'The Cost of the Current Contact Model' and 'A Redesigned Service Model' state topics, not findings. Visually it is a competent but stock report skin: thin blue rule under each H1, a bordered key-takeaways box, one bordered table, one stat trio; nothing in the type or the grid says transport authority or service redesign, and the same shell would serve any consulting assessment unchanged.

Integrity holds: no clipping, overflow or placeholder text anywhere; page 5 ends cleanly with notes and sources and the trailing whitespace reads as a document end, not a broken page. Legibility is fine for a partner-facing A4 report, though the body type on pages 2-5 is small relative to the generous margins and the chart axis labels on page 3 are near the floor of comfortable print size. Coherence is strong: the same running header (title left, section label right), the same footer triplet (Confidential — Partner Group / page x of 5 / date), the same navy rule under each H1, and consistent figure/table captioning with sources beneath each. Communicative effectiveness is where it earns level 4: every page title is a conclusion, not a label — 'Hiring alone closes only 62% of the gap', 'The plan costs $3.8m more than today's run rate' — and the KPI strip on page 2 (400 / 17% / 26% / 62%) is correctly unit-labelled with a source line. Page 3's chart has a figure number, a takeaway line under it and a source. Page 4's bridge table carries FTE units in every column header and a Method callout explaining the 17% blend. It stops short of level 5 for two specific reasons. First, the page 3 chart is the weakest artefact in the deck: it is a three-bar net-headcount column chart with a single-series legend ('Net headcount') that carries no information, and it shows the endpoint of the bridge rather than the bridge itself — the gross hires and attrition that the surrounding prose spends three paragraphs on are invisible, so the one chart in the document does not carry the document's central argument. A waterfall would have. Second, the composition is one column of stacked prose on every page with no variation in rhythm; pages 2-5 look like the same slot filled four times, and pages 3, 4 and 5 leave the lower half to two-thirds of the sheet empty, which reads as a page-per-section rule rather than a deliberate pace. On genericness: the numbers are specific to the brief and the KPI strip, bridge table and cost delta table are shaped by this problem, but the frame around them — navy rule, KPI strip, key-takeaways bullets, notes-and-sources tail — is a chassis that would look identical for a pricing plan or an ops review. I would send it, with a fixed chart.

Integrity holds across all ten pages: no clipped tables, no placeholder text, no overlap. The page-3 bar chart sits inside its column with axis labels intact; the page-5 headcount bridge table and the page-9 cost table both fit their measure. Legibility is fine — single-column body at a comfortable measure, dark blue/black on white, running header and footer repeat identically on pages 2–10. Coherence is strong: consistent rule under each H1, consistent table styling (thin header rule, right-aligned numerics), consistent figure caption + source line format ('People & Talent Strategy workforce model, September 2026') on nearly every exhibit. Communicative effectiveness is where it earns its level: titles conclude rather than label — 'Why hiring alone falls short of the target', 'Attrition is concentrated, not even', 'What the plan costs against the current run rate' — the page-2 KPI trio (400 / 62% / 26%) each carries a caption, the page-5 bridge reconciles beginning/attrition/gross hires/ending with a shortfall sub-table, and page-9 gives per-head and three-year incremental cost against run rate. Numbers carry units (pts, $, headcount) and page 10 closes with a numbered source list. It stops short of level 5: page 1 is a nearly empty cover with a thin rule and four lines of text, a lot of dead space for a partner-facing document; page 3's chart is the only graphic in ten pages, so pages 4, 6, 7, 8 read as long prose blocks with one small table each, and the page-7 '19%' stat sits alone and undersized relative to the page-2 KPI treatment — the same idea rendered two different ways. The blue accent, generous white margin and rule-under-heading system are a competent but familiar consulting-report shell; what makes it feel specific to this brief is the content (tenure-band attrition table, junior/senior mix table, the bridge), not the design.

Integrity and legibility hold: nothing is clipped or placeholder, the header/footer band, blue rule and type sizes are consistent, and the KPI trio on page 2 (160 FTE / 26% / 62%) carries units. Titles are conclusion-shaped ('The three-to-five-year band drives disproportionate attrition risk', 'The headcount bridge shows retention closing 38% of the gap'), the Figure 1 grouped bar chart has both a takeaway line and an 'Illustrative planning model, People & Talent Strategy, Sept 2026' source, and the FY27–FY29 bridge table on page 4 has beginning HC, leavers, hires needed, filled today and ending HC with its own source note. Where it fails is density against purpose: pages 2, 3 and 4 all stop at roughly half the page height with the footer stranded far below, and page 5 — the recommendation, the page partners actually act on — runs six lines of prose plus a one-item notes list and then leaves the bottom 45% blank. The brief asked what the plan costs against the current run rate, and the only answer is the qualitative 'low single-digit percentage of the current staff cost run rate' on page 5 plus the 'Costing caveat' box on page 4; there is no cost table or figure anywhere, which is the one number the managing partners will look for. The cover is also thin — rule, title, subtitle, date, confidentiality line and nothing else. Coherent and clean, but under-built for the ask, so it stops at level 3.
